newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Exiled king plans return to anarchic Albania.
newsitem.headline: Exiled king plans return to anarchic Albania.

text.p: Albania's exiled king, who has spent only a few days of his life in his Balkan homeland, plans to return in an effort to help calm the turmoil there, a monarchist party leader said on Wednesday.

Guri Durollari of the Legality Movement told Reuters King Leka I, who lives in South Africa, was planning to fly to Albania on Saturday. Albanian political parties agreed on Wednesday during a round-table meeting with President Sali Berisha to permit the exiled ruler to return.
"I am sure that King Leka I will influence very positively the present situation in Albania," Durollari said. "The King is Albanian and his homeland is looking for him after 58 years."
Leka Zogu, 58, was only a few days old when his father, King Zog, fled the country with his family in 1939.

Albania has been plunged into near chaos since get-rich-quick investment schemes collapsed earlier this year and armed rebels took control of the south of the country during an unchecked spasm of looting and banditry.
Durollari said the king, who grew up with Albanian exiles and speaks the language, could help restore peace and stability.
"He is the national symbol and a possible unifying factor at this moment," Durollari said.

Last month the king said in an interview with Reuters at his ranch-style home outside Johannesburg he was assessing the situation in his troubled homeland hour by hour and preparing to return at any time.

"King Leka I is non-allied with any party and at this moment all the parties, which agree on a referendum to define the form of governing -- republic or monarchy, should find a consensus to revive life in Albania," he said.

Though it is questionable how much support the king would have in a country he left as an infant, Leka said such a referendum should come before elections in June, rather than the other way around as proposed.
Leka said he opposed the armed insurrection gripping the country, describing it as part civil disobedience, part mob rule. "There are lots of armed bands who have no political axe to grind," he said.

Leka, tall and bespectacled, tried to visit Albania in 1993, saying he recognised the legitimacy of republican rule. Authorities bundled him back onto a private aircraft within 24 hours of his arrival on the grounds that his passport marked "Kingdom of Albania" was invalid.
Durollari said on Wednesday in Tirana the king would arrive "with a private aeroplane from a Mediterranean country". He declined to say whether he would come with his old passport.
Leka has said he would like to see the creation of a "Greater Albania", which would include Albanian regions in Kosovo and Greece. He was proclaimed king when his father died in Britain in 1961.
